summary: Specifies ways to communicate route exclusions when setting up paths with RSVP-TE. It builds on RFC 3209 and the GMPLS extensions of RFC 3473, which allow explicit route hints, and lets a requester say which nodes or links the path must avoid. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: When planning a trip, you can say, go anywhere except through that muddy road. This lets a network path request say what places to avoid.

subtitle: How a path request can tell RSVP-TE routers which nodes, links and risk groups the path must avoid.

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE lets a path request list the hops a path should include, but it has no way to say which nodes or resources the path must stay away from. That matters when the head end does not compute the full route itself.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4874 adds an EXCLUDE_ROUTE object (XRO) that lists what to avoid on the whole path, and an Explicit Exclusion Route subobject (EXRS) that lists what to avoid between two hops of an explicit route. It also adds an SRLG subobject so whole Shared Risk Link Groups can be excluded.
tldr.outcome: Routers expanding loose hops now know what they must not use, so diverse backup paths can be set up across areas and autonomous systems. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 6001 and RFC 8390.

today: RFC 4874 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473, and it has itself been updated by RFC 6001 and RFC 8390, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why Paths Need an Avoid List
sections.content:
RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) and its GMPLS extensions (RFC 3473) let a path request name abstract nodes and resources that must be included, using the Explicit Route Object (ERO). They cannot say that something must be excluded.

That gap matters in networks where the head end does not compute a precise explicit path. Loose hops and abstract nodes get expanded later by other routers, and those routers may need to be kept away from a specific resource. A typical case is two non-overlapping Label Switched Paths (LSPs): set up the first, record its route, then exclude those routers when setting up the second.

The RFC defines two kinds of exclusion. The Exclude Route list applies to the whole path. The Explicit Exclusion Route applies only between a specific pair of abstract nodes in an ERO. Each gets its own encoding, described below.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally you can only tell a navigator where to go. This RFC lets you also say where not to go, either for the whole trip or just for one stretch of it.

sections.title: What Exclusion Is Meant to Do
sections.content:
An exclusion is not meant to describe the actual route by listing every hop to skip. The intent is to signal only the minimal number of things to avoid, for example just the SRLGs, so that the normal route selection process (such as expanding a loose hop) is constrained.

The RFC walks through a path across three areas, A, B and C. A node-diverse protection path has to avoid every node on the primary path. The ingress handles area A itself during its Constrained Shortest Path First (CSPF) computation, so the signaled exclusion list starts with the border node into area B. At each area border the router can strip entries that no longer matter, and at the last border it can drop the list entirely because it can expand a full strict path to the destination.

Implementers are reminded, as with explicit routes, to consider the size of the signaled data and its impact on the signaling protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: You do not have to list every road you want to avoid, just the important ones. As the trip moves along, you can cross items off the list once they are behind you.

sections.title: The EXCLUDE_ROUTE Object and Its Subobjects
sections.content:
Abstract nodes to avoid are carried in the EXCLUDE_ROUTE object (XRO), which uses Class 232 and C_Type 1. Its contents are a series of variable-length subobjects, adapted from the ERO subobjects of RFC 3209, RFC 3473 and RFC 3477. The supported subobject types are IPv4 prefix (1), IPv6 prefix (2), Unnumbered Interface ID (4), Autonomous system number (32) and the new SRLG subobject (34).

Strict and loose have no meaning for exclusion, so the L bit is reused. A value of 0 means the abstract node MUST be excluded. A value of 1 means it SHOULD be avoided: the path must not traverse a node listed with L clear, but may traverse one listed with L set, and routing nodes should minimize how many of those it uses.

The IPv4, IPv6 and Unnumbered Interface ID subobjects gain an Attribute octet. A value of 0 means the interface or set of interfaces, 1 means the whole node, and 2 means all the SRLGs associated with that interface. This lets a requester exclude a whole node by naming just one of its interfaces, or exclude one interface without excluding the node.

The SRLG subobject is new. An SRLG identifier is a 32-bit quantity (as defined in RFC 4202). The subobject has type 34 and a fixed Length of 8, followed by a reserved field that SHOULD be zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt. For exclusions its L bit is read as the exclude or avoid choice described above.
sections.plainLanguage: The avoid list is a list of little notes, each naming a road, a town, a whole region, or a group of roads that could all be blocked together. Each note also says whether you absolutely must skip it or just should if you can.

sections.title: How Routers Process the XRO
sections.content:
When a Path message arrives, a node checks whether it is itself a member of any abstract node in the XRO that is marked exclude. If so, it SHOULD return a PathErr with error code Routing Problem and error value Local node in Exclude Route. A node should also check its resources against any SRLGs in the XRO. A subobject that does not make sense, such as an IPv4 prefix holding a node address but with the attribute set to interface, draws Inconsistent Subobject.

If the ERO and XRO contradict each other, a mandatory exclusion (L clear) takes precedence: the node MUST reject the Path message with Route blocked by Exclude Route. A contradiction with an avoid entry (L set) is optional: the node MAY reject, or MAY carry on and ignore that XRO subobject.

When choosing a next hop or expanding an explicit route, a node MUST NOT introduce any node or SRLG-identified resource that the XRO marks as exclude, and SHOULD minimize those marked avoid. A node may also reject an XRO that is too large or complicated for local policy, with error value XRO Too Complex, and the ingress may then simplify it or route around that node.

The XRO class number has the form 11bbbbbb, so routers that do not understand it forward it untouched. That lets exclusion cross parts of the network that cannot parse it, and Record Route can help a computing node spot violations. When forwarding, a node may add an XRO, remove it, or add and remove subobjects, but it MUST NOT list in the XRO a node it has also put in the ERO.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router along the way checks the avoid list. If it finds that it is on the list, or that the next step would use something on the list, it sends the request back with a note saying why it cannot go on.

sections.title: Explicit Exclusion Route Between Two Hops
sections.content:
The second kind of exclusion is carried inside the ERO. The Explicit Exclusion Route Subobject (EXRS) is a new ERO subobject of type 33. It wraps one or more subobjects whose format is exactly the same as in the XRO, so it can exclude nodes, Autonomous Systems, unnumbered interfaces, link ids, labels or SRLGs. An EXRS MUST NOT appear inside an XRO. Its own L bit MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

The scope of an EXRS is only the step between the previous ERO subobject that names an abstract node and the next one. The processing rules are the same as for the XRO within that scope, and several exclusions may sit between the same pair of nodes.

A node that does not support exclusions treats an EXRS like any unrecognized ERO subobject and returns a PathErr with Bad EXPLICIT_ROUTE object. A supporting node may refuse an overly complex EXRS with EXRS Too Complex.

If both an XRO and an EXRS apply, the node MUST honor everything listed in both places. Where they overlap, the stricter request wins: if one list says must exclude and the other only says avoid, the element is excluded.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you only want to skip something for one stretch of the trip, like avoiding a bridge between two towns. The EXRS is a note tucked into the route between those two towns that applies just there.

sections.title: Minimum Compliance
sections.content:
The RFC sets a floor for implementations. The XRO MUST be supported. The IPv4 Prefix subobject MUST be supported with a prefix length of 32 and attribute values of interface and node, and the IPv6 Prefix subobject MUST be supported with a prefix length of 128 and the same attribute values. Other prefix lengths and attributes MAY be supported.

The EXRS is optional. If supported, the same restrictions apply. If not, an EXRS met during normal ERO processing MUST be rejected as an unknown subobject. A node SHOULD NOT parse ahead in the ERO, and if it does, it MUST NOT reject the ERO on finding an EXRS that applies to some other node.

Whatever a node does support, it MUST follow the processing rules for supported, unsupported and partly supported subobjects. A node that supports the XRO but not a particular subobject, or part of one, simply ignores that subobject.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router has to understand the basic avoid list for single addresses. The fancier between-two-towns notes are optional, but a router that does not understand them has to say so rather than guess.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new messages and no substantive new processing, so the security considerations of RFC 3209 and RFC 3473 continue to apply. Anything that worries a domain about explicit routes should also be considered for exclusions: a boundary that strips EROs from Path messages should also consider removing the XRO.

One specific risk is denial of service. An arbitrarily complex XRO or EXRS sequence causes extra work at every node on the path. The RFC notes that this assumes an otherwise trusted router, one authenticated by its neighbors, is misbehaving. A node that finds an XRO or EXRS too complex under local policy can respond with the matching Too Complex error.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky sender could write a giant, confusing avoid list to keep routers busy. Routers are allowed to say a list is too complicated and send it back.

sections.title: Applications: Protecting Paths
sections.content:
The appendix shows that one generic object serves several uses. In inter-area protection, the ingress picks a different area border router for the backup LSP and includes an XRO listing the primary path's nodes in the later areas, so each border router can expand the ERO disjointly. Each border router may drop entries for the area it has just handled, but must keep the border router where the primary path leaves the area. With link or node protection, the XRO length is bounded by the length of the primary LSP's Record Route Object.

For inter-AS protection, the same method works when the backup follows the same AS path with different ASBRs. If it does not, the XRO should always carry the full primary path. SRLG ids only help if the ASs share a consistent SRLG space; otherwise the inter-AS link address can go in the XRO and the entering ASBR can translate it into local SRLG ids.

In the GMPLS overlay model, an edge node can set up several LSPs to the same destination with few or no SRLGs in common, or a backup that also protects the links between edge nodes and core nodes. Inside a single area without IGP traffic engineering extensions, the XRO can exclude the links, nodes or SRLGs of the primary LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: The main use is making a backup route that does not share anything risky with the main route, so if one breaks the other still works.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Loose or strict for explicit routes; for exclusions it SHOULD be zero and is ignored.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length in bytes including Type and Length; always 8.

fields.name: SRLG Id (first 16 bits)
fields.desc: First half of the 32-bit SRLG identifier.

fields.name: SRLG Id (last 16 bits)
fields.desc: Second half of the 32-bit SRLG identifier.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: SHOULD be zero on transmission, MUST be ignored on receipt.

items.desc: Has a prefix length and an Attribute octet.

items.desc: TE Router ID and Interface ID, with an Attribute octet.

items.label: EXRS
items.desc: Explicit Exclusion Route subobject; allowed in an ERO, never in an XRO.

items.label: SRLG
items.desc: Identifies a Shared Risk Link Group to exclude or avoid.
